_comment: The six book-club contenders. Numbers are from each book's Goodreads page (the edition on the Want to Read shelf). 'year' is original publication. 'kindred' lists authors on your read shelf with a real literary link, used at half weight when you haven't read the author themselves. 'discussion' is a hand-scored 0-100 for how much a group will have to argue about.

candidates.title: The Turn of the Screw
candidates.author: Henry James

kindred.author: Diane Setterfield
kindred.why: Setterfield writes in James's Victorian ghost-story tradition

kindred.author: Algernon Blackwood
kindred.why: Blackwood was James's contemporary in the English ghost-story boom

candidates.discussionWhy: Are the ghosts real or is the governess unravelling? Critics have argued about this for 125 years, and your group will too.
candidates.caveat: Late-Henry-James sentences are famously dense; short, but not fast.

candidates.title: Dark Harvest
candidates.author: Norman Partridge

kindred.author: Ray Bradbury
kindred.why: Partridge's Halloween small town is a deliberate riff on Bradbury's Something Wicked This Way Comes

candidates.discussionWhy: A town that feeds its boys to an annual Halloween ritual: conformity, violence and who benefits from tradition. Bram Stoker Award winner.
candidates.caveat: Pulpy second-person voice and a lot of gore; plays more like a movie than a novel.

candidates.title: Pet Sematary
candidates.author: Stephen King

kindred.author: Algernon Blackwood
kindred.why: King borrowed Blackwood's Wendigo as the thing behind the burial ground

candidates.discussionWhy: The best-known horror novel about grief. Would you walk up that path? What do we owe the dead, and what do we tell our kids about death?
candidates.caveat: The longest pick by far, and the death of a child is central. Check the room before proposing it.

candidates.title: The Halloween Tree
candidates.author: Ray Bradbury
candidates.discussionWhy: A whirlwind tour of how cultures (Egypt, Celtic Britain, Notre-Dame, Día de Muertos) have faced death. Good for comparing traditions.
candidates.caveat: Written for young readers, so there's less to chew on for adults than the others.

candidates.title: Harvest Home
candidates.author: Thomas Tryon
candidates.discussionWhy: The American Wicker Man: city family, perfect New England village, corn-goddess cult. Gender power, nostalgia and 1970s back-to-the-land anxieties.
candidates.caveat: Slow-burn first half; some 1970s gender politics that will read as dated (which can itself be a discussion).

candidates.title: The Hill of Dreams
candidates.author: Arthur Machen

kindred.author: Algernon Blackwood
kindred.why: Machen and Blackwood were fellow Golden Dawn members and the twin pillars of Edwardian weird fiction

kindred.author: Jorge Luis Borges
kindred.why: Borges championed Machen and picked him for his own 'Library of Babel' anthology series

candidates.discussionWhy: A lonely young writer, a Roman ruin in Wales and a mind dissolving into visions. Is it horror at all? A good debate about art and isolation.
candidates.caveat: Hardly any plot, and hard to find in stores: only about 1.5k Goodreads ratings.
